name: Psyllium husk

card.summary: Gel-forming soluble fibre from Plantago seed husks; well studied for constipation and cholesterol, with only minor weight-loss effects reported.
card.aka: Ispaghula, isabgol, Plantago ovata husk, Metamucil (brand)
card.note: Needs adequate fluid to avoid choking or obstruction; 2024 testing found lead in all nine psyllium supplements tested.

quick.overview:
Psyllium is a viscous soluble fibre made from the seed coat of Plantago species, mainly Plantago ovata, grown largely in northern India. It is a long-standing over-the-counter fibre supplement and is used in baking and as a food thickener.

It is also marketed as a fullness aid for weight control. Wikipedia cites a 2023 review reporting only minor weight loss over 12 weeks in people with overweight or obesity, from low-to-moderate quality studies. Its better-supported effects are on constipation, LDL cholesterol and blood sugar.
quick.mechanism: Psyllium is not absorbed by the small intestine. It absorbs water to form a gel that softens stool and adds bulk. The fullness effect proposed by marketers is attributed to the same gel; the mechanisms behind its cholesterol and blood-sugar findings are not detailed in the sources reviewed.
quick.risks: Common effects are gas, bloating and abdominal pain. Taken with too little water it can thicken in the throat and cause choking or bowel obstruction. Allergic reactions including anaphylaxis occur, especially among people occupationally exposed to the powder. Wikipedia reports that ConsumerLab found lead in all nine psyllium supplements it tested in 2024.

lead: Psyllium, also called ispaghula or isabgol, is obtained from seeds of Plantago species, chiefly Plantago ovata. The seed coat is milled into a white husk that absorbs water to form a gel; the gel-forming polysaccharide has been characterised chemically. [1][2] India produces most of the world supply. [1]

It is best known as a fibre supplement for constipation and, in the US, as the active ingredient in Metamucil, introduced by G.D. Searle in 1934 and later acquired by Procter & Gamble. [1] Trials and meta-analyses have also examined its effect on cholesterol and blood glucose. [3][4][5]

Psyllium is marketed for weight loss on the basis of fullness, but Wikipedia reports that a 2023 review found only minor weight loss over 12 weeks in overweight or obese people, based on low-to-moderate quality evidence. [1]
infobox: Seed husk of Plantago ovata and related species [1]

paras: Psyllium softens stool and reduces straining, and is considered more a fibre than a stimulant laxative. Wikipedia cites a 2021 review that found modest effects with a generally good safety profile, and a 2022 review that found it increased weekly bowel movements more than osmotic and stimulant laxatives over at least four weeks. [1] A double-blind randomised trial reported on the effects of dietary fibres or probiotics on functional constipation and gut microbiota. [7] Another study examined psyllium husk's effect on intestinal microbiota in constipated patients and healthy controls. [8]

subs.h: Cholesterol, blood sugar and blood pressure
paras: A meta-analysis of eight controlled trials found cholesterol-lowering effects of psyllium added to diet therapy in people with high cholesterol, and a longer-term study reported similar findings. [3][9] A trial in men with type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol reported effects on glucose and lipids, and another study reported lower serum glucose and HbA1c in diabetic outpatients. [4][5]

The US FDA authorised a health claim linking psyllium soluble fibre to reduced heart disease risk in 1998, and a qualified claim about type 2 diabetes in 2014 with a disclaimer that evidence is very limited. [1] A 2019 meta-analysis reported about a 2 mmHg blood-pressure reduction in people with hypertension. [1]
Supplements are sold for satiety and weight control. Wikipedia reports only minor weight loss over 12 weeks in a 2023 review. [1]

Psyllium has more human trial data than most fat-loss supplements, but most concern constipation, cholesterol and glucose rather than appearance. Registered studies include psyllium seed and body weight in people with schizophrenia (NCT06789471, 24 participants), psyllium husk in children and adolescents with metabolic syndrome (NCT00748787, terminated), and fibre and gut microbiota (NCT05906589, 40 participants). [10][11][12] For weight loss, Wikipedia cites a 2023 review reporting minor effects. [1]

Gas, bloating and abdominal pain are common. Without enough fluid psyllium can thicken in the throat or cause bowel obstruction and bezoars. [1] Psyllium can cause allergic reactions including anaphylaxis, and healthcare workers exposed to psyllium laxatives show high rates of sensitisation. [1]

In 2024 ConsumerLab reported lead in all nine psyllium supplements it tested, with four above alert thresholds. A 2013 California settlement required a manufacturer to add warning labels for lead. Contamination is largely soil-derived, so organic products are also affected, and Wikipedia advises buyers to look for batch-specific heavy-metal testing. [1]

The Indian brand Sat-Isabgol went on sale in 1937. G.D. Searle introduced Metamucil in 1934, initially sold behind the counter so pharmacists could advise buyers. Procter & Gamble acquired it in 1985, and flavoured versions arrived in 1979. [1]
